title: Building a little test plan
idea: MEET. For a whole solution, list the cases worth checking: a normal case, the empty case, the boundary. Reason about coverage.

exercises.prompt: For 'count scores >= 50', a solid little test plan is...
exercises.explanation: A normal mix, the empty list, and the exact boundary 50 together cover the everyday case, the nothing case, and the cutoff.
options: A normal mix, an empty list, and a score of exactly 50

exercises.prompt: A good test plan covers the normal case AND the awkward cases, not just one of them.
exercises.explanation: Yes — coverage means the common path and the corners. Testing only one leaves the others unproven.

exercises.prompt: For 'average with empty guard', which case MUST be in the plan?
exercises.explanation: The empty list is the whole reason the guard exists, so it must be tested or the guard is unproven.
options: A list of all the same value only

exercises.prompt: For 'highest bid', a thorough plan includes a list where the max is...
exercises.explanation: Testing the max at the start, middle, AND end proves the update logic works wherever the biggest value sits.
options: First, middle, and last in different test lists

exercises.prompt: Match each test case to what it proves.
exercises.explanation: Each case has a job: normal proves the everyday path, empty proves the guard, boundary proves the comparison.

exercises.prompt: Your plan has three cases and all three match their expected answers. What can you conclude?
exercises.explanation: You have good evidence it works for those cases. 'Proven for the cases tested' is honest — more cases give more confidence.
options: Strong evidence it's correct for the cases you covered
Absolute proof for every possible input
That it will never have a bug

exercises.prompt: Passing three well-chosen cases guarantees the code is bug-free for ALL inputs.
exercises.explanation: No — tests give evidence, not a mathematical guarantee. But well-chosen cases catch the vast majority of real bugs.

exercises.prompt: Order how to run a test plan.
exercises.explanation: List the cases with expected answers, run each, compare each, then judge the whole solution. Coverage then verdict.
blocks: List the cases and their hand-worked answers
Run the code on each case
Compare each output to its expected answer

exercises.prompt: One case fails, two pass. The overall verdict is...
exercises.explanation: Any failing case means the solution is not yet proven — fix the bug, then re-run the whole plan. One fail = fail.
options: Fail — fix the bug and re-run all cases

exercises.prompt: Why write the test plan as a LIST before running anything?
exercises.explanation: Listing cases first stops you from only testing what you know works; it forces you to include the awkward ones.
options: It forces you to include the awkward cases, not just the easy one
